summary: This unit is about getting on well with the people you work with: sharing information clearly, listening, keeping your commitments, helping the team reach its goals, respecting differences, and giving and taking feedback. You will also learn to solve problems before they grow, to recognise and report bullying, harassment and discrimination, to welcome new staff, and to stay professional with co-workers and clients when the salon is busy.

blocks.p: This unit covers the people side of salon work: how you speak, listen, behave and solve problems with the people around you. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, but the same skills are needed in a barber shop, a spa, a hotel or any other workplace.

A salon is a small team working close together in a small space, in front of clients, often under pressure. When the team gets on well, the day runs smoothly, clients feel welcome and they come back. When it does not, clients soon notice the lateness, the gossip and the arguments, and they take their business elsewhere. **Good working relationships are part of good service.**

What this means in the salon
rows: Know your role and the workplace rules
Understand your contract, your job description, the rota and the salon's policies
Know who to go to with a request or a problem
Share information clearly
Take part in briefings; use the appointment book, record cards and notice board
Pass on messages accurately and check they were understood
Ask questions when you are not sure
Listen well and use positive body language
Give your full attention and let people finish
Sum up and ask questions to check
Work towards the team's goals
Know the goals and keep your commitments
Take part in meetings and share ideas the proper way
Help others when you are free
Show respect and build trust
Be honest, reliable and polite
Respect differences in age, culture, religion and ability
Behave professionally
Be on time, neat and discreet
Keep private information private
Keep proper boundaries with clients
Give and receive feedback
Give it privately, about the work, with an example
Receive it calmly, ask questions and use it
Deal with problems and conflict
Raise problems early, calmly and in private
Take them to the supervisor, and then the grievance procedure, if they are not solved
Protect and support others
Recognise and report bullying, harassment and discrimination
Help new staff settle in
Keep good relationships in busy times

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks. In one, your group holds a team meeting and agrees a fair rota and team plan. In the other, you role-play common workplace problems, solve them and fill in an issue record. The assessor watches how you speak, listen and behave, not only what you write.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In role plays, use only the made-up names on the cards. Never act out real people from the Centre, and stop at once if anyone becomes upset.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The salon team and the workplace rules

blocks.p: You cannot work well with people unless you know who does what. A **co-worker** (or colleague) is anyone who works with you for the same employer. Each one has a role, and each role depends on the others.

head: Role
Main duties
How you work with them
rows: Owner or manager
Runs the business; sets the goals, prices and rules; hires staff; deals with serious complaints.
Respect their decisions. Take serious problems to them through the proper steps.
Supervisor (often a senior stylist)
Plans the rota and the day; checks work; trains juniors.
Usually the first person you go to with a request, a problem, an absence or an accident.
Stylists, barbers and nail technicians
Carry out the services; may train juniors.
Learn from them; help when asked; do not take their clients or tools.
Junior stylists and assistants
Shampoo, prepare stations, help the seniors, clean and restock.
Do your fair share and ask when you are unsure.
Receptionist
Books appointments, answers the phone, greets clients, takes payments and messages.
Tell her early if you are running late; give her accurate times; act on her messages.

blocks.note: In some Jamaican salons and barber shops, stylists rent a chair and work for themselves instead of being employees. They are still part of the team: they share the space, the rules, the equipment and the clients' trust.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: The papers that set out your job

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: Contract of employment
The agreement between you and your employer: your job, pay, hours, leave and notice. Read it before you sign it and keep your copy.
Job description
The list of your duties and the person you report to.
Staff handbook or salon policies
The rules on hours, breaks, lateness and absence, uniform, phones, conduct, health and safety, harassment, discipline and complaints.
Rota (roster)
The chart that shows which staff work on which days and shifts. Check it every week.
Duty list
Who does each shared job, such as the laundry, cleaning the basins and restocking, and on which day.

blocks.p: **Workplace culture** means the shared values and ways of behaving in a workplace: 'how we do things here'. You can feel it in how staff greet each other, how problems are handled, whether people help one another and whether the rules are kept. Every member of staff helps to make the culture, including the newest junior.

ul: Jamaican employment law gives workers rights on matters such as pay (at least the national minimum wage), hours, leave, and fair treatment when a job ends.
The **Ministry of Labour and Social Security** deals with work, wages and employment matters. It can advise workers and employers and help to settle disputes that cannot be solved in the workplace.
Jamaica's data protection law says that personal information about clients and staff must be kept private and secure.
Jamaica has a law to protect people from sexual harassment at work. Employers are expected to have a policy on it and a way for staff to complain.

blocks.note: Always try the salon's own steps first: the co-worker, then the supervisor, then the owner and the grievance procedure. Outside help is for problems that cannot be solved inside, or that are too serious to wait.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Good communication keeps clients safe and the day running. If the receptionist learns that a client is allergic to a product, the stylist must know before she mixes anything. If a stylist is running 20 minutes late, reception must know so the next client can be told. Information that stays in one person's head helps nobody.

head: Method
Good for
Take care
rows: Briefing (huddle): a short meeting at the start of the day
The day's bookings, special requests, staff changes, stock problems and the day's target.
Be on time. Keep it short. Note the points that concern you.
Face to face
Quick questions, and anything that needs an answer now.
Choose your moment: not in the middle of a client's service unless it is urgent. Speak quietly about private matters.
Appointment book or booking system
Who is booked, when, with whom and for what; notes such as 'skin test due'.
Write neatly. Date and initial any change.
Client record cards
Allergies, past services, products and reactions.
Private: only for the staff who need them.
Notice board
The rota, the rules, training dates and team goals.
Check it every day. Never post private information.
Message book or message slip
Messages for someone who is busy or out.
Write who it is from, the number, the message, when a reply is needed, the date and time, and your name.
Staff group chat or phone message
Quick changes: a late client, a delivery, a swapped shift that has been approved.
Keep it about work. No client details or photos without consent. Not while you are with a client.

ul: Give the key facts: **who, what, when and where**. 'Mrs Grant, colour retouch, moved from 2:00 to 3:30 today, with Karen.'
Keep it short. Leave out what the person does not need.
Give clock times and dates, not 'later' or 'next week some time'.
For a co-worker who is busy with a client, a short written note with the facts and the time is clearer than calling across the salon.
Check that it was understood: ask the person to repeat the main point, or repeat it back yourself when you are the one receiving it.
Written notes are neat, dated and signed or initialled.
Pass on anything about safety, such as an allergy, **at once and in person**, and write it on the record card as well.

blocks.note: 'Soon come' and 'just now' mean different lengths of time to different people. At work, say the time: 'I will be back at 1:15.'
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: If you do not understand an instruction, ask questions until you do, then say it back in your own words. Guessing wastes time and products, and with chemicals it can harm a client.
Nobody thinks less of a trainee who asks. They think less of one who pretends to know.

A request to change your hours, swap a shift or take a day off goes **directly to the supervisor or owner** who plans the rota, in good time. Do not arrange it only with a co-worker, and do not send it through someone else.
The salon's rules on breaks, uniform, lateness and conduct are in the staff handbook or policies. Read them, and ask if something is not clear.

blocks.p: The same words can help or hurt, depending on how they are said. Keep your tone **calm and polite even when you are busy**: say please and thank you, keep your voice down on the salon floor, and never snap at a co-worker in front of clients. Use words the other person understands. Many of us move easily between Jamaican Creole (Patois) and Standard English; with clients, visitors and in anything written, use clear Standard English, and never make fun of the way anyone speaks.

Hearing is not the same as listening. Listening means giving the speaker your attention, understanding what she means and how she feels, and showing her that you have understood. Most quarrels at work get worse because one person feels she was not heard.

flow: Stop what you are doing, if you can, and put your phone away
Face the person and give comfortable eye contact
Let her finish: do not interrupt or finish her sentences
Think about her words, not about your reply
Sum up what you heard
Ask questions to check
Agree what happens next

head: Body language
The message it usually sends
rows: Facing the person, arms relaxed and uncrossed, leaning in slightly
I am open and interested.
Comfortable eye contact, nodding now and then
I am paying attention. Go on.
A calm, interested face
I take you seriously.
Crossed arms, a frown, a turned back
I am closed off, annoyed or not interested.
Looking at your phone, the clock or the mirror while she talks
You are not important to me.
Sighing, rolling the eyes, kissing the teeth
I have no respect for what you are saying.
Standing over someone, pointing a finger, hands on hips
I am angry and ready to argue.

blocks.note: Kissing your teeth or giving someone a 'cut-eye' says a great deal without a word, and can start a quarrel faster than anything you say. Keep both out of the workplace.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Body language is a guide, not a rule. Some people look down out of respect or shyness, and some cross their arms because they are cold. Look at the whole person, and ask if you are unsure how she feels.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Skill
Example
What it does
rows: Summing up (saying it back in your own words)
'So the towels are running out by three o'clock on Saturdays?'
Checks that you understood, and shows her that you listened.
Open question
'What would make Saturdays easier for you?'
Brings out more information and ideas.
Closed question
'Can you start at 8:30 on Friday?'
Gets a fact or a yes or no.
Showing you understand her feelings
'I can see why that upset you.'
Calms the person. You can do this even when you do not agree with her.

ul: **Noise**: dryers, music and several conversations at once. Move somewhere quieter for anything important.
**Being busy or tired**: say, 'Give me two minutes to finish this, then you will have my full attention.'
**Judging the speaker**: deciding she is wrong before she has finished.
**Planning your reply** while she is still talking.
**Hearing loss or a different first language**: face the person, speak clearly at a normal pace, do not shout, and write down key points such as times and amounts.

blocks.p: A team has **goals**: results that everyone is working towards. You find out the goals by listening at meetings and briefings, reading the notice board and asking your supervisor. Then you help in your daily work.

head: Team goal
How a junior stylist can help
rows: More clients who come back
Give every client careful, friendly service, and offer to book her next visit before she leaves.
More retail sales
After the service, suggest products that suit her hair and explain how to use them. Be honest; never push.
Shorter waiting times
Arrive on time, have your station ready, tell reception early if you are running late, and help others when you are free.
A clean, safe salon
Do your jobs on the duty list without being reminded, and report hazards and faulty equipment.
A new service
Attend the training, practise, and ask for feedback.

ul: A commitment is a promise: you do **what you said you would do, when you said you would do it**.
Do not promise what you cannot deliver. It is better to say, 'I can do it by Thursday, not Tuesday.'
If something stops you, tell the person or your supervisor **early**, and offer another plan. A late warning lets everyone down.
Being on time for your shift is a commitment too. One late stylist means waiting clients and co-workers who must cover.
When a client cancels or you have a gap, offer to help a co-worker or the receptionist instead of sitting on your phone.

blocks.p: Meetings are where the team shares ideas and agrees its plans. Take part: listen, speak up politely, and stick to the point.

head: Meeting word
What it means
rows: Agenda
The list of items to be discussed, in order, often with a time for each. It is shared before the meeting.
Chair
The person who leads the meeting: keeps to the agenda, gives everyone a turn and sums up what was agreed.
Minute-taker
The person who writes down who was present, what was decided and who will do what.
Timekeeper
The person who watches the clock and warns the chair when time for an item is nearly up.
Minutes
The written record of what was agreed at the meeting.
Action list
Each job that was agreed: **who** will do it, **what** exactly, and **by when**.

flow: Agenda shared
Meeting opens; roles agreed
Each item discussed; everyone heard
Decisions agreed
Actions given: who, what, by when
Minutes written and shared
Actions checked at the next meeting

blocks.p: A useful action is exact. Compare 'Someone should look into the towels' with this action list:

head: Action
Who
By when
rows: Order 3 dozen hand towels from the supplier
Miss Clarke (supervisor)
Wednesday 3 December
Make up 20 gift packs and price them
Kadian
Friday 5 December
Put the cleaning duty list for December on the notice board
Andre
Monday 1 December

blocks.p: If you have an idea, for example a better way to store the towels or cut waiting times, raise it at a staff meeting or with your supervisor. Say what the problem is, what you suggest and how it helps the salon. Do not just change the way things are done on your own, and do not complain to clients or other staff that 'nobody listens'. If your idea is not chosen, accept it and keep contributing.

ul: Every busy time is covered by enough staff with the right skills.
Everyone gets proper breaks, and nobody is planned for long hours day after day without rest.
Late shifts, weekends and the less popular days are shared fairly.
Religious days, study times and family duties are respected where the work allows, and those staff take a fair share of other busy shifts.
It is agreed and posted in good time. Swaps are approved by the supervisor before they happen.

blocks.note: Seventh-day Adventists keep the Sabbath from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday; many other Christians worship on Sunday morning. Plan these into the rota from the start. The busiest salon weeks are usually Christmas and New Year, Easter, graduation season and the back-to-school rush in late August, so agree those rotas early.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Cooperation** means working together and helping each other. A fair rota works only if people cooperate: each person gives a little, a compromise is reached, and everyone keeps to what was agreed.

ul: Greet people, and say please and thank you.
Use the name each person prefers, in a polite tone: 'Miss Campbell' if that is what she likes, a pet name only if she has told you she likes it.
Listen to other people's views and value them, even when you disagree.
Ask before you use anyone's tools, products or station, and return them clean.
Respect people's time: be punctual and finish what you start.
Thank a co-worker who helps you. It shows that you value her and builds good will, so people are glad to help again.

blocks.p: Trust is the belief that a person will be honest with you and do what she says. It grows slowly, through many small acts, and it can be lost in a moment. **Once trust is lost it is very hard to rebuild.**

head: Builds trust
Destroys trust
rows: Telling the truth, including about your own mistakes
Lying, hiding mistakes or blaming others
Doing what you promised, on time
Breaking promises; often being late
Doing your fair share of shared jobs
Leaving your work for others
Keeping private things private
Gossiping and passing on secrets
Giving others credit for their work and ideas
Taking credit for someone else's idea
Speaking to a person directly and politely about a problem
Talking behind her back
Respecting other stylists' clients, tools and products
Taking another stylist's regular clients, tools or products

blocks.p: **Diversity** means the differences between people: age, sex, colour, culture, religion, ability and disability, where they come from, how they speak, and their family life. A salon team is diverse, and so are its clients. A mixed team is a strength: people bring **different ideas and skills**, such as natural hair care, braiding, barbering or experience with older clients, so the salon can serve everyone well.

head: Difference
Respectful behaviour
rows: Age
Listen to younger and older staff equally. Do not assume an older person cannot learn a new method or that a young person has nothing to teach.
Religion
Allow for days of worship, dress and food rules when you plan the rota or a staff lunch. Ask the person; do not guess. Do not argue about beliefs.
Culture and where people come from
No jokes about 'country' people, other parishes, other islands or other countries. Be curious, not mocking.
Accent and language
Never imitate or laugh at the way someone speaks. If you do not understand, ask politely.
Disability or a health condition
Ask what helps, and offer help without taking over. Do not talk about the person as if she were not there.
Sex and family life
Share jobs by skill, not by whether someone is a man or a woman. Do not pry into private lives.

blocks.note: Food can exclude people without anyone meaning it. Many Rastafari do not eat pork and keep an ital diet, Seventh-day Adventists and Muslims do not eat pork, and some co-workers are vegetarian or have allergies. When you plan a staff lunch, ask each person and make sure there is something everyone can eat.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A **bias** is an unfair leaning for or against a person or a group, such as giving the best shifts to your friends.
A **stereotype** is a fixed idea about a whole group: 'young people are lazy', 'men cannot do nails'.
**Discrimination** is acting on bias: treating someone unfairly because of who they are.
Being fair does not always mean treating everyone exactly the same. It means giving each person what she needs to do the job, such as written instructions for a co-worker who is hard of hearing.
If you see someone being mocked or left out, do not join in. Support the person, and speak up or report it.

blocks.p: Professional conduct is how you behave at work every day, whether or not anyone is watching. Clients judge the whole salon by it, and your co-workers depend on it.

head: Area
What professional looks like
Why it matters
rows: Time and attendance
On time for every shift, back on time from breaks. If you are sick or delayed, phone the supervisor before your shift starts.
Clients and co-workers are not let down, and the rota can be changed in time.
Appearance
The salon's uniform, clean and neat; good personal hygiene; hair and nails that advertise your skills.
You represent the salon.
Phone
On silent and put away while you are with clients, unless the salon uses phones for bookings.
The client is paying for your attention.
Language
Polite, with no swearing or shouting across the floor.
Clients hear everything.
Gossip
You do not start it, pass it on or listen to it.
It hurts people, breaks down trust and makes clients wonder what is said about them.
Honesty
With money, tips, products, stock and your time.
Missing stock or cash damages trust in everyone.
Fitness for work
Never at work under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
You handle chemicals, heat and sharp tools.

ul: Clients talk while you work. What you hear about their health, family, money or relationships is **kept private and not repeated**, not to co-workers, not to other clients and not at home.
Record cards are stored safely and seen only by the staff who need them.
The same goes for what you know about your co-workers: pay, health and personal problems are theirs to share, not yours.

**Consent** is a person's agreement, given before you do something that affects her. Ask for it before you photograph a client or a co-worker, and again before you post the picture. Follow the salon's rules on photos and social media.
If someone asks you about another client, a polite answer is: 'I am not able to talk about other clients.' Then change the subject.

blocks.p: Be friendly with clients, but remember that the relationship is a business one.

ul: Give every client the same good service, not only friends or big tippers.
Keep conversation suitable for work. Stay out of arguments about politics, religion and other people.
Do not borrow money from clients or lend it, and do not give out your home address.
Do not take the salon's clients for private work at home unless your contract and the owner allow it. It is unfair to the salon and breaks its trust in you.
If a client makes unwanted advances or rude remarks, say no politely and firmly, and tell your supervisor. You do not have to put up with it to keep a client.

blocks.note: Keeping boundaries protects three parties at once: the client, you and the salon's good name.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Feedback is information about how well a piece of work was done, given so that the person can keep doing what is good and improve what is not. Given well, it is a normal and useful part of work. Given badly, it damages the relationship.

flow: Choose a private place and a suitable time
Start with something that went well
Describe the work or behaviour, with a real example
Explain its effect
Suggest a way forward
Ask for her view
Agree what happens next

head: Instead of...
Say...
rows: 'You are so careless.'
'The colour bowl was left unwashed at station 2 yesterday, and it had set hard by this morning.'
'You are always late.'
'You came in at 9:20 on Tuesday and Thursday, and Mrs Bailey had to wait both times.'
'That roller set was rubbish.'
'The rollers at the crown were too big for her hair length, so the curl dropped. Let me show you the size I would use.'
Saying nothing, then complaining to others
'Can I mention something about the towels? I think there is an easier way.'

ul: Listen to all of it without interrupting, arguing or making excuses.
Ask questions if you do not understand, or ask to be shown: 'Which part should I change?'
Thank the person, even when it is hard to hear.
Think about it honestly, then use it. Ask for more training if you need it.
If you disagree, or the way it was given upset you, say so calmly and in private, later if you need time to cool down.

blocks.p: A **conflict** is a serious disagreement or clash between people. In salons the usual causes are shared stations left untidy, borrowed tools, who gets the walk-in client, the rota, cleaning duties, lateness that others must cover, taking another stylist's client, and gossip. Small problems that are ignored grow into big ones, so deal with them early.

head: Style
What it looks like
Example
Result
rows: Passive
You say nothing, or hint, and hope it stops.
'It's all right, don't worry about it.'
The problem carries on and you grow resentful.
Aggressive
You attack the person: shouting, blaming, insults, threats.
'You are too nasty! Don't touch my things again!'
A quarrel; the other person defends herself and nothing is solved.
Assertive
You say clearly and with respect what the problem is and what you need.
'I feel stressed when I find hair in my clippers. Please brush them out after you use them.'
The best chance of an answer both can accept.

blocks.p: An **'I' statement** is the simplest assertive tool. It talks about the behaviour and how it affects you, not about what kind of person she is: **'I feel... when... Could we...?'** Words such as 'you always' and 'you never' start arguments.

blocks.h: Steps for solving a problem with a co-worker

flow: Calm down first
Check the facts and the salon's rules
Choose a private place and a time when neither of you is busy
Explain the problem with 'I' statements
Listen to her side without interrupting
Look for an answer you can both accept
Agree it, note it and try it
Check after a week or two
Not solved? Take it to the supervisor
Still not solved? Use the grievance procedure

ul: Often the rules already hold the answer. Before two stylists argue over a walk-in client, check the salon's rota or rule for walk-ins.
A **win-win** answer is one in which both sides gain something. A **compromise** is where each side gives up a little to reach agreement.
The supervisor's job is to listen to both sides, check the facts and the rules, and help them agree a fair solution. She may change the rota or the station plan.
A **mediator** is a neutral person who helps two sides in a dispute to reach their own agreement. She does not take sides or decide who wins.
A **grievance procedure** is the salon's written set of steps for raising a serious complaint, usually in writing, to the owner or manager.
Throughout, stay polite, do not gossip about it and never involve clients.

blocks.note: If a co-worker is angry and shouting, do not shout back. Stay calm, keep your voice low and ask to talk somewhere private, or later when you are both calmer. If you feel unsafe, walk away and tell the supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

head: On the issue record form
Example
rows: Date, and who was involved
14 November; R. Thomas and K. Lewis
What happened (facts only)
Station 3 left with hair on the floor and used towels on the chair at the 2:00 p.m. hand-over, on 10, 12 and 14 November.
Steps taken
Spoke privately on 14 November at 4:30 p.m.
Outcome
Agreed a hand-over check list: floor swept, towels in the bin, tools cleaned, by 1:50 p.m.
Follow-up
Review on 28 November. Supervisor informed.

sections.title: Bullying and harassment, new staff and busy times

head: Word
What it means
Examples
rows: Bullying
Repeated behaviour meant to hurt, frighten or put a person down.
Shouting, insults and name-calling; mocking; leaving someone out on purpose; always giving her the worst jobs; spreading rumours.
Harassment
Unwanted behaviour that offends, upsets or humiliates a person, often because of her sex, colour, religion, age or disability.
Jokes about a person's religion or disability; offensive messages or pictures; following someone around.
Sexual harassment
Unwanted behaviour of a sexual kind.
Unwanted touching; sexual remarks or jokes; staring; repeated requests for dates after 'no'; asking for sexual favours in return for shifts or a job.
Discrimination
Treating a person unfairly because of who she is.
Refusing to hire or train someone because of her age, religion or disability; giving a man better pay than a woman for the same work.

blocks.p: These behaviours can come from co-workers, managers or clients. 'It was only a joke' is no excuse: what matters is that the behaviour is unwanted and hurtful.

flow: If you feel safe, tell the person clearly that the behaviour is unwelcome and must stop
Write down what happened, when, where and who saw it
Keep any messages
Report it to your supervisor or the owner, as the salon's policy says
If the supervisor is the problem, go to the owner or another manager
Use the grievance procedure if it continues
Get outside advice if the salon does not act

blocks.h: If you see it happen to someone else

ul: Do not join in or laugh.
Support the person: speak to her, and let her know you saw it.
Report it, following the salon's policy. Offer to say what you saw.
Do not spread the story as gossip.

blocks.p: **Induction** (or orientation) is the period when a new worker is shown the workplace, its rules and her duties. A good first week makes a confident team member; a bad one makes mistakes and resignations.

ul: Welcome her, introduce her to everyone by name and say what each person does.
Show her around: stations, basins, dispensary, laundry, stock room, staff area, bathroom, fire exits, first-aid kit.
Explain how things work: the rota, the duty list, breaks, the booking system, where tools and products are kept, how to report a problem.
Name one person she can ask, and check on her during the day.
Be patient with questions and mistakes. Everyone was new once.
Include her at break times, and never leave all the unpleasant jobs to 'the new girl'.

blocks.p: At busy times, such as the weeks before Christmas, everyone is tired and small problems turn into arguments. The team that plans ahead and keeps talking gets through it.

ul: **Plan together** before the rush: the rota, the breaks and who does which cleaning and restocking jobs.
**Keep your commitments** and be on time: one late person makes the day harder for all.
Keep messages **short, clear and polite**, however full the salon is.
**Help** a co-worker when you have a gap, and say thank you when you are helped.
Do not take your stress out on co-workers or clients.
If you are overloaded, **tell the supervisor early** instead of getting angry.
Take your breaks, drink water and eat. A hungry, tired stylist is a short-tempered one.
Put any disagreement aside until a quiet moment, then talk it through in private.
I can name the roles in a salon team and say who to go to with a request or a problem.
I can explain what a contract of employment, a job description, a staff handbook, a rota and a duty list are.
I can name three ways staff share information and say how to make a message clear.
I can pass on a message with the key facts and check that it was understood.
I can describe how to listen well, including what I do with my body and what I say.
I can read common body language and say what message it sends.
I can explain how a junior stylist helps the salon reach its goals.
I can describe the roles of the chair, the minute-taker and the timekeeper, and write an action with who, what and by when.
I can say what makes a rota fair.
I can list the behaviours that build trust and those that destroy it.
I can explain why differences in age, culture, religion and ability matter, and give examples of respectful behaviour.
I can describe professional conduct, confidentiality, consent and boundaries with clients.
I can give feedback privately, about the work, with an example, and receive feedback calmly.
I can tell passive, aggressive and assertive behaviour apart, and make an 'I' statement.
I can list the steps for solving a problem with a co-worker, up to the grievance procedure.
I can define bullying, harassment, sexual harassment and discrimination, and say what to do if I experience or see them.
I can help a new co-worker settle in.
I can explain how to keep good relationships during busy, stressful times.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give an example from a salon for each point, and say why it matters. For example: 'I give feedback in private, so that my co-worker is not embarrassed in front of clients.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Co-worker (colleague)
A person who works with you for the same employer.
Contract of employment
The agreement between a worker and an employer that sets out the job, pay and hours.
Job description
The document that lists the duties of a job.
Staff handbook (policies)
The salon's written rules on matters such as breaks, uniform and conduct.
Rota (roster)
The chart that shows which staff work on which days and shifts.
Workplace culture
The shared values and ways of behaving in a workplace.
Briefing (huddle)
A short meeting at the start of the day where the team agrees the plan.
Agenda
The list of items to be discussed at a meeting.
Chair
The person who leads a meeting.
Minutes
The written record of what was agreed at a meeting.
Action list
The jobs agreed at a meeting: who, what and by when.
Commitment
Something you have promised to do.
Cooperation
Working together and helping each other.
Active listening
Giving full attention, letting the person finish, then summing up and asking questions to check.
Body language
The messages sent by your posture, face, eyes and gestures.
Trust
The belief that a person is honest and will do what she says.
Diversity
The differences between people, such as age, culture, religion and ability.
Bias
An unfair leaning for or against a person or a group.
Stereotype
A fixed idea about everyone in a group.
Discrimination
Treating someone unfairly because of who they are.
Confidentiality
Keeping private information private.
Consent
A person's agreement, given before you do something that affects her.
Feedback
Information about how well work was done, given to help the person improve.
Conflict
A serious disagreement or clash between people.
Assertive
Saying what you need clearly and with respect.
'I' statement
A way of raising a problem that describes the behaviour and how it affects you: 'I feel... when...'.
Win-win
An answer to a disagreement in which both sides gain something.
Compromise
An agreement in which each side gives up a little.
Mediator
A neutral person who helps two sides in a dispute to reach an agreement.
Grievance procedure
The steps for raising a serious complaint at work.
Bullying
Repeated behaviour meant to hurt, frighten or put a person down.
Harassment
Unwanted behaviour that offends or upsets a person.
Sexual harassment
Unwanted touching, remarks or requests of a sexual kind.
Induction (orientation)
The period when a new worker is shown the workplace, its rules and her duties.
Ministry of Labour and Social Security
The Jamaican government ministry that deals with work, wages and employment matters.

c1.title: Planning back-to-school week in Linstead
c1.text: A salon in Linstead, St Catherine, expects its busiest week of the year in late August, when parents bring their children for cornrows and trims before school opens. The owner, Mrs Gloria Henry, calls a staff meeting with a written agenda and chairs it. Stylist Marcia Dixon is a Seventh-day Adventist and does not work from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday. Nail technician Kerry-Ann Lyn has evening classes on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The team's goal is that no client waits more than 15 minutes past her booked time.

c2.title: A shared flat iron in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Shanelle and Tanisha are stylists who share a station at a salon in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. Shanelle works mornings and Tanisha works afternoons. Three times this week Shanelle has arrived to find her own flat iron on Tanisha's side of the station with product burnt onto the plates. Today two clients are waiting and Shanelle is angry. She plans to 'tell Tanisha about herself' the moment she walks in at one o'clock.

c3.title: A new shampoo assistant in Port Antonio
c3.text: Odane, 19, has just started as a shampoo assistant at a busy salon in Port Antonio, Portland. He is hard of hearing in his left ear and wears a hearing aid. The salon plays music all day and the dryers are loud. On his first morning nobody showed him where the towels or the disinfectant are kept. By Thursday, senior stylist Dwayne is calling him 'Deafy', gives him every dirty job, and laughs with others when Odane asks for something to be repeated.

c4.title: A regular client in Falmouth
c4.text: Mrs Joan Ellis has her hair relaxed every six weeks by Simone, a stylist employed at a salon in Falmouth, Trelawny. While Simone works, Mrs Ellis tells her that she is going through a divorce and has a health problem. Later another client asks Simone, 'What is wrong with Mrs Ellis? She looks so stressed.' Mrs Ellis has also asked Simone to come to her house on Sundays and do her hair 'cheaper than the salon'. Simone would like to post a photo of Mrs Ellis's new style on her own social media page.

c5.title: After a busy Saturday in Old Harbour
c5.text: At a salon in Old Harbour, St Catherine, junior stylist Tameika finished a silk press 25 minutes late on Saturday, so her next client had to wait. The supervisor, Miss Brown, said loudly in front of two clients, 'Tameika, you are too slow. You will never make it as a stylist.' Tameika was embarrassed and has been upset all weekend. On Monday morning Miss Brown asks to see her in the office to talk about Saturday.

questions.q: What is the fairest way to plan Marcia into the rota for the busy week?
o: Roster her for Saturday too, because the week is too busy for exceptions
Keep her off Friday evening and Saturday, and give her other busy shifts
Give her the whole week off, so that nobody has to plan around her
Let the team vote on whether her Sabbath should count in a week like this
questions.why: Respecting a co-worker's day of worship is part of treating her fairly, and it is planned in from the start. She takes a fair share of other busy shifts, so the load is still shared.

questions.q: While Kerry-Ann is explaining her class times, a junior stylist keeps talking over her. What should Mrs Henry do as chair?
o: Move to the next agenda item and leave Kerry-Ann's point out
Let them both talk, since the meeting will finish sooner
Ask him to let her finish, then give him his turn to speak
Tell him off sharply so the whole team learns the lesson
questions.why: The chair's job is to keep order and make sure everyone is heard in turn. She does it politely: embarrassing someone in front of the team damages the relationship.

questions.q: Which entry in the minutes is the most useful action?
o: Combs: everybody agreed that the salon needs more of them
Somebody to sort out more combs before school opens
Mrs Henry thinks combs could be a problem in August
Rojay to buy 24 wide-tooth combs by Friday 22 August
questions.why: A useful action says who will do it, exactly what, and by when. The others name no person or no date, so nobody is responsible and nothing can be checked at the next meeting.

questions.q: At the meeting Kerry-Ann agreed to make up 30 packs of hair bands and clips by Friday. On Wednesday she learns she has an extra class and cannot finish them. What should she do?
o: Tell Mrs Henry now, and suggest a helper or a new time
Finish what she can and say nothing unless she is asked
Leave a note with the unfinished packs on Friday evening
Ask a classmate to make them, without telling the salon
questions.why: Keeping a commitment includes warning people early when you cannot meet it, and offering another plan. A late surprise lets the whole team down in its busiest week.

questions.q: When and where should Shanelle raise the problem with Tanisha?
o: At one o'clock on the salon floor, while it is fresh in her mind
In the staff group chat, so that everyone can see what happened
At the next staff meeting, without speaking to Tanisha first
In the staff room later, when neither of them has a client
questions.why: A problem is raised with the person herself, in private, when both are calm and free. Doing it in front of clients or the whole team embarrasses her and turns a small problem into a quarrel.

questions.q: Which opening is assertive, rather than passive or aggressive?
o: 'You always spoil my things. You have no respect for anybody else.'
'I get upset when my iron is left dirty. Can we agree a rule?'
'It's nothing really. Forget I said anything about the iron.'
'Who told you that you could touch my iron? Answer me.'
questions.why: An assertive opening describes the behaviour and its effect on you, then asks for what you need, with respect. 'You always' and demands are aggressive; saying it is nothing is passive.

questions.q: Tanisha explains that she thought the iron belonged to the salon. They agree that Shanelle will label her tools and keep them in her drawer, and Tanisha will use the salon's iron and clean it. Why is this a good outcome?
o: Shanelle has shown Tanisha who is in charge of the station
The supervisor never has to know there was a problem
Tanisha has admitted that everything was her fault
Each of them gains something, and the cause is removed
questions.why: This is a win-win: Shanelle's tools are protected and Tanisha has an iron to use, so both gain and the misunderstanding cannot happen again. The aim is to fix the problem, not to win.

questions.q: A month later the problem returns, and Shanelle decides to take it to the supervisor. What will help the supervisor most?
o: A short note of the dates, what happened and what was agreed
A list of all Tanisha's other faults since she joined the salon
Statements from clients who have seen the untidy station
A message in the group chat asking the team to take sides
questions.why: The supervisor needs facts: what happened, when, and what has already been tried. Bringing in other faults, clients or the rest of the team is gossip and makes a fair solution harder.

questions.q: What is the best way to give Odane instructions in the salon?
o: Call them loudly across the floor so they carry over the dryers
Give them to another assistant, who can pass them on to him
Face him, speak clearly at a normal pace and check he has them
Send them all to his phone, so that nobody needs to speak to him
questions.why: Facing a person who is hard of hearing, speaking clearly without shouting and checking he has understood removes the barrier. Passing messages through others loses details, and avoiding speaking to him shuts him out of the team.

questions.q: Which would have helped Odane most on his first morning?
o: A price list to study quietly during his lunch break
A tour, the rules, his duties and a named person to ask
A week of watching before he was allowed any questions
A written test on shampoo products before he started
questions.why: A proper induction shows a new worker the workplace, its rules and his duties, and gives him someone to turn to. Without it he wastes time, makes mistakes and feels unwelcome.

questions.q: How should Dwayne's treatment of Odane be described?
o: Harmless teasing that every new worker learns to take
Normal training, since juniors start with the dirty jobs
A private matter that the two of them should sort out
Bullying: it is repeated and meant to put him down
questions.why: Name-calling about a disability, always giving one person the worst jobs and laughing at him, again and again, is bullying and harassment. Calling it a joke does not change that, and the salon must not accept it.

questions.q: Odane has asked Dwayne to stop, but it goes on. This week the supervisor is on leave and Dwayne is in charge. Who should Odane report it to?
o: The owner or another manager, as the salon's policy sets out
Nobody until the supervisor is back, however long that takes
The clients, so that they can complain on his behalf
Dwayne, in writing, as he is acting as the supervisor
questions.why: When the person in charge is the one causing the problem, the report goes to the owner or another manager. He should also keep a dated note of each incident and who saw it.

questions.q: What is the best reply to the client who asks what is wrong with Mrs Ellis?
o: 'She has a lot going on at home, but I can't tell you more than that.'
'I'm not able to talk about other clients. How is your hair today?'
'You should ask her yourself. She tells everybody her business.'
'I'll tell you, but you must promise to keep it to yourself.'
questions.why: What a client shares during a service is private. Even a hint ('a lot going on at home') passes on her business; a polite refusal and a change of subject protects her and shows the other client that her own secrets are safe too.

questions.q: How should Simone answer the request for cheaper Sunday visits at Mrs Ellis's home?
o: Agree, because what she does on a Sunday at home is her own affair
Agree, as long as Mrs Ellis keeps it secret from the salon
Decline politely, as private work with its client wrongs the salon
Agree, and offer the same price to her other salon clients
questions.why: Mrs Ellis is the salon's client, and Simone is its employee. Taking her away for private work, unless the contract and the owner allow it, breaks the owner's trust and may break her contract.

questions.q: What must Simone do before she posts the photo of Mrs Ellis's hair?
o: Crop the photo so that only part of her face is showing
Post it on her own page only, not on the salon's page
Wait a week, so nobody links the photo with the visit
Get Mrs Ellis's consent and follow the salon's rules
questions.why: A person's image is her own: she must give consent before a photo is taken and before it is posted. The salon's rules on photos and social media apply to staff pages too.

questions.q: Which comment from Miss Brown would have been the most useful feedback?
o: 'The press ran 25 minutes over. Let's go over your timing.'
'Tameika, everybody in here can see just how slow you are today.'
'You need to do better. I won't tell you again after this.'
'Some people are just not made for this kind of work.'
questions.why: Useful feedback is about the work, gives a real example and points to a way forward, and it is given in private. Comments about the person, made in front of clients, only embarrass her and teach nothing.

questions.q: Tameika wants Miss Brown to know how Saturday's remark affected her. What is the best way?
o: Work slowly all week, so that Miss Brown notices she is upset
Tell the clients next Saturday how badly she was spoken to
Say calmly in the office how it felt to hear it before clients
Post about it online, without naming the salon or Miss Brown
questions.why: A concern is raised with the person directly, calmly and in private, using an 'I' statement such as 'I felt embarrassed when it was said in front of clients.' Sulking, involving clients or posting online damages trust and her own name.

questions.q: In the office Miss Brown asks, 'What do you think went wrong on Saturday?' Which answer shows the most professional attitude?
o: 'Nothing went wrong. That client's hair is just too thick.'
'The other stylists run late too, and nobody says a word to them.'
'I misjudged the time, and I should have warned reception early.'
'I don't know. You are the supervisor, so you should tell me.'
questions.why: Owning a mistake honestly and seeing what to do differently builds trust and lets the supervisor help. Blaming the client or co-workers, or refusing to think about it, does the opposite.

questions.q: Two barbers cannot agree on how to share Saturday walk-in clients, and the owner asks a neutral person from outside the shop to sit with them. What is that person there to do?
o: Decide which barber is right and announce the result
Help both of them work out an agreement of their own
Report to the owner on which barber should be dismissed
Speak for the barber who has worked there the longest
questions.why: A mediator is neutral: she helps each side to explain, listen and find an answer both accept. She does not judge, take sides or punish.

questions.q: A salon owner turns down a skilled nail technician for a job only because she is 52 and 'the team is young'. What is this an example of?
o: Discrimination
Mediation
Induction
Compromise
questions.why: Treating a person unfairly because of who she is, here her age, is discrimination. A decision about a job should rest on skills, qualifications and conduct.
